qs.q: A patient with erythema migrans and multi-organ involvement is diagnosed with Lyme disease. Which vector is responsible for transmitting the causative agent, Borrelia burgdorferi?
qs.e: Borrelia burgdorferi, the causative agent of Lyme disease, is transmitted by ixodid (hard) ticks, particularly Ixodes species.

qs.q: People living in forested areas are at a risk of Lyme disease, which is transmitted by ticks, often found in wooded and grassy environments.
qs.e: Lyme disease is a tick-borne illness caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi. Ticks, particularly Ixodes species, are commonly found in forested areas, as well as in grassy and bushy habitats, making people who frequent these environments at higher risk of exposure.

qs.q: Lyme disease is transmitted by ticks, Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever by ticks, and Plague by fleas. Malaria is transmitted by mosquitoes.
qs.e: Malaria is transmitted by mosquitoes, while Lyme disease and Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever are transmitted by ticks, and Plague is transmitted by fleas. Therefore, malaria is the odd one out in terms of its primary vector.

ai.title: Lyme Disease
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: A tick‑borne spirochete infection presenting in stages, from erythema migrans to neuro‑cardiac complications. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion and serology; treatment is doxycycline or amoxicillin.

sections.p: Lyme disease is caused by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi, transmitted by Ixodes ticks. In East Africa the disease is uncommon but should be considered in patients with unexplained rash, fever or arthralgia after outdoor exposure.

B. burgdorferi is a gram‑negative, spiral‑shaped spirochete that grows slowly in low‑oxygen environments. It expresses outer surface protein C (OspC) during early infection and B (OspB) in later stages.
Ixodes ticks acquire the spirochete from infected small mammals. The tick must feed for 24–48 h to transmit the organism. Humans are accidental hosts.
Lyme disease progresses through three stages: early localized (erythema migrans), early disseminated (multiple rashes, meningitis, carditis), and late chronic (arthritis, chronic neurologic disease).

Clinical diagnosis is paramount. When EM is present, serology is unnecessary. In later stages, a two‑tiered serology (ELISA followed by Western blot) is recommended. In low‑resource settings, a rapid IgM/IgG test may be used with caution.

t.b: Positive ELISA → confirm with Western blot
Positive bands (IgM 23‑30 kDa, IgG 39‑41 kDa) confirm diagnosis

sections.p: Remember that a single EM rash is diagnostic; serology is not needed. In resource‑poor settings, treat clinically if history and rash are classic. Watch for cardiac conduction blocks and meningitis in disseminated disease.
Chronic fatigue syndrome, viral arthralgia, rheumatic fever, and other tick‑borne illnesses can mimic Lyme disease.
Early serology may be negative; IgM can persist for months, leading to false positives. In endemic malaria areas, anemia may mask hematuria.
If a patient presents with acute heart block or meningitis, start doxycycline immediately and arrange ECG and lumbar puncture if available. Supportive care and monitoring of vitals are essential.

faq.q: What is the classic rash of Lyme disease?
faq.a: Erythema migrans – a circular, expanding rash often with a central clearing.

faq.q: Can Lyme disease be cured with antibiotics?
faq.a: Yes, early treatment with doxycycline or amoxicillin usually cures the infection.

faq.q: Why is serology not needed in stage I?
faq.a: Because the rash is pathognomonic and antibodies may not yet be detectable.

exam: A patient with a history of tick exposure develops new-onset atrioventricular block – what is the likely diagnosis and treatment? — Lyme carditis; start doxycycline and monitor ECG; consider temporary pacing if severe.

A child presents with migratory polyarthritis and a history of outdoor activity – what serologic test is most appropriate? — ELISA followed by Western blot; if ELISA negative, consider repeat in 2 weeks.

A patient with chronic fatigue and arthralgia is found to have positive IgM but negative IgG – what does this indicate? — Early infection or false positive; consider clinical picture and repeat serology.
A patient with Lyme disease in a low‑resource setting cannot access ELISA – what is the clinical approach? — Treat based on history and EM rash; if unavailable, use rapid IgM/IgG test with caution.
